articles.description: Enums enhance code readability but can lead to errors if not validated, as any integer can be cast as an Enum, including invalid values. Validating Enum inputs prevents silent data corruption, ensures meaningful defaults, and avoids processing impossible states. Always validate at method boundaries and define a zero value as "unknown."
articles.title: Defensive Programming Rule #3: Validate Your Enums (Every Time)

articles.author: dotNetDave
articles.description: Parameter validation is crucial in programming, ensuring applications reject bad data before it causes issues. It safeguards data integrity, reduces bugs, and enhances developer satisfaction. The use of meaningful exceptions and tools like Spargine can standardize validation, while adopting strategies like nameof improves error messaging accuracy. Consistent validation fosters reliable APIs.
articles.title: Defensive Programming Rule #2: Always Validate Method Parameters

articles.author: dotNetDave
articles.description: Defensive programming emphasizes anticipating potential failures in code, treating every line as a possible error point. Developers should use structured exception handling, provide meaningful error messages, and maintain system integrity. Tools like Spargine facilitate effective defensive programming by simplifying error handling and promoting resilience in applications by addressing unexpected scenarios.
articles.title: Defensive Programming Rule #1: Anticipate Errors and Eliminate Bugs

articles.description: Soft delete is one of the most enduring patterns in enterprise systems: instead of permanently removing rows from your database, you mark them as deleted. This preserves history, enables audits, supports undo operations, and keeps your system safe from accidental “delete catastrophes.” In this deep dive, we implement a maintainable soft-delete architecture using EF Core, global query filters, and a clean, generic repository.
articles.title: Don’t Drop the Data: Engineering a Robust Soft Delete Pattern in EF Core

articles.description: SQL Server 2025 introduces new observability tools, improved TempDB I/O governance, hybrid buffer pool enhancements, and smarter columnstore metadata. All these changes amplify the benefits of row, page, and columnstore compression. This in-depth technical guide explains how data compression works in SQL Server 2025, what has changed, and includes full hands-on T-SQL examples, test scripts, and best practices for DBAs and developers.
articles.title: SQL Server 2025 Compression Deep Dive: Internals, Performance Gains & Real-World Benchmarks

articles.description: The transaction log is one of SQL Server’s most misunderstood components. Undersize it and your system chokes on autogrowths; oversize it and your storage team complains about wasted space. Let’s cut through the myths and build a methodical way to size your transaction log properly, based on recovery model, workload, and backup strategy.
articles.title: Sizing Your Transaction Log in SQL Server: How Big Is Big Enough?

articles.author: fofo
articles.description: Checkpoints in SQL Server are often misunderstood. Contrary to popular belief, they don’t only flush committed data they write all dirty pages, even from uncommitted transactions. Transactional safety comes from the log and recovery process, not from checkpoint filtering.
articles.title: SQL Server Myth: “Checkpoint Only Writes Pages from Committed Transactions”

Last week, we released version 2.0 of dotnet-script. The latest release introduces support for .NET 10.0 and C# 14 and is available, as usually, through Github releases and on Nuget. You will need to have at least the .NET SDK 10.0.100 installed.
It is the first major release of dotnet-script since version 1.0, which was released back in 2020. At the same time, the breaking changes are minimal, and the revision is mostly driven by the careful application of semantic versioning principles.
